claims.text: Point-of-care ultrasound can improve diagnostic accuracy and help distinguish an abscess from cellulitis when there is diagnostic uncertainty
claims.quote: Point-of-care ultrasound can improve diagnostic accuracy and help distinguish an abscess from cellulitis when there is diagnostic uncertainty (2).

claims.text: Diagnosis is usually clinical: a suggestive history and painful, tender, fluctuant erythematous swelling
claims.quote: The diagnosis of cutaneous abscess is usually based on clinical evaluation. Supportive clinical findings of a cutaneous abscess include a suggestive history and painful, tender, and fluctuant erythematous swelling on examination.

claims.text: Gram stain and culture are generally recommended, primarily to identify MRSA and get susceptibilities
claims.quote: Gram stain and culture are generally recommended, primarily to identify MRSA and obtain antimicrobial susceptibility testing (1).

claims.text: Look-alikes: hidradenitis suppurativa and ruptured epidermal cysts (rupture releases keratin, causing an inflammatory reaction sometimes resembling infection; culture seldom reveals pathogens); perineal abscesses may be a deeper perirectal abscess emerging or drainage from Crohn disease via a fistula
claims.quote: Conditions that resemble simple cutaneous abscesses that are usually recognizable clinically (including on a rectal examination) include hidradenitis suppurativa and ruptured epidermal cysts. Epidermal inclusion cysts (often incorrectly referred to as sebaceous cysts) rarely become infected; however, rupture releases keratin into the dermis, causing an exuberant inflammatory reaction sometimes clinically resembling infection. Culture of these ruptured cysts seldom reveals any pathogens. Perineal abscesses may represent cutaneous emergence of a deeper perirectal abscess or drainage resulting from Crohn disease via a fistulous tract.

claims.text: Causes A localized, usually well-defined collection of pus within the skin
claims.quote: Cutaneous abscesses are localized, usually well-defined collections of pus within the skin.

claims.text: Risk factors: skin barrier disruption, injection drug use, bacterial overgrowth, antecedent trauma (particularly with a foreign body), immunosuppression, impaired circulation
claims.quote: Risk factors for cutaneous abscesses include the following: Skin barrier disruption Injection drug use Bacterial overgrowth Antecedent trauma (particularly when a foreign body is present) Immunosuppression Impaired circulation

claims.text: Organisms are typically skin or nearby mucosal flora: S. aureus (including MRSA) and streptococci are common causes on the trunk, extremities, axillae, head and neck (can be polymicrobial); perineal abscesses carry stool organisms, commonly anaerobes or mixed aerobes and anaerobes
claims.quote: Bacteria causing cutaneous abscesses are typically commensal or colonizing organisms originating from the skin of the involved area or from adjacent mucous membranes. S. aureus (including MRSA) and streptococci continue to be common causes of abscesses on the trunk, extremities, axillae, and head and neck; these can also be polymicrobial. Abscesses in the perineal (ie, inguinal, vaginal, buttock, perirectal) region contain organisms found in the stool, commonly anaerobes or a combination of aerobes and anaerobes (see table ).

claims.text: Symptoms Painful, tender, indurated and usually erythematous; typically 1 to 3 cm, sometimes much larger; firm at first, then as it points the skin thins and feels fluctuant (fluctuance may be obscured in very deep abscesses); may drain spontaneously
claims.quote: Cutaneous abscesses are painful, tender, indurated, and usually erythematous. They vary in size, typically 1 to 3 cm in length, but are sometimes much larger. Initially the swelling is firm; later, as the abscess points, the overlying skin becomes thin and feels fluctuant. Fluctuance is a key feature when present; however, in very deep abscesses, fluctuance may be obscured by overlying soft tissue. The abscess may then spontaneously drain.

claims.text: Local cellulitis, lymphangitis, regional lymphadenopathy, fever and leukocytosis are variable accompanying features
claims.quote: Local cellulitis, lymphangitis, regional lymphadenopathy, fever, and leukocytosis are variable accompanying features.

claims.text: Some small abscesses resolve without treatment, and warm compresses help; incision and drainage is indicated when significant pain, tenderness and swelling are present; it is unnecessary to await fluctuance
claims.quote: Some small abscesses resolve without treatment, coming to a point and draining. Warm compresses help accelerate the process. Incision and drainage is indicated when significant pain, tenderness, and swelling are present; it is unnecessary to await fluctuance.

claims.text: After the pus drains, bluntly probe the cavity to clear loculations; irrigation is optional; loose gauze packing reduces dead space (wick typically removed after 24 to 48 hours), but data suggest routine irrigation or packing is unnecessary for abscesses < 5 cm
claims.quote: After the pus drains, the cavity should be bluntly probed with a gloved finger or curette to clear loculations. Irrigation with normal saline is optional. Packing the cavity loosely with a gauze wick reduces the dead space and prevents formation of a seroma. The wick is typically removed 24 to 48 hours later. However, data suggest that routine irrigation or packing for abscesses < 5 cm in diameter is unnecessary (2, 3).

claims.text: Antibiotics were traditionally reserved for systemic infection, cellulitis, multiple abscesses, immunocompromise, or a facial abscess in the cavernous sinus drainage area: empiric anti-MRSA therapy (eg, sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, clindamycin; vancomycin if severe) pending culture; later studies suggest fewer failures and recurrences when antibiotics are added for any abscess needing treatment where MRSA is prevalent
claims.quote: Antibiotics have traditionally been considered unnecessary unless the patient has signs of systemic infection, cellulitis, multiple abscesses, immunocompromise, or a facial abscess in the area drained by the cavernous sinus. In these cases, empiric therapy should be started with a medication active against MRSA (eg, sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, clindamycin; for severe infection, vancomycin) pending results of bacterial culture. However, subsequent studies have suggested lower rates of treatment failure and recurrence when antibiotics are added for any abscess that requires treatment in locations where MRSA is prevalent (4).
